campaign_platform_points: Economy & cost of living: The campaign proposes eliminating school district property taxes on homeowners via constitutional amendment, appraising properties only once every five years, lowering the homestead appraisal cap from 10% to 3%, requiring two-thirds voter approval for local tax increases, and capping local government spending at population plus inflation or 3.5%.

Criminal justice & public safety: The campaign pledges to expand the repeat offender taskforce, deny bail to illegal immigrants arrested for violent felonies, establish a statewide prosecutor to support or replace local DAs, and allow impeachment of district attorneys who fail to prosecute violent criminals.

Housing: The campaign proposes cutting red tape in homebuilding by allowing third-party inspections, requiring 10-day occupancy determinations, pre-approving home designs across cities, allowing property additions by right, and withholding sales tax from cities that undermine housing reforms with luxury mandates.

Healthcare: The campaign proposes capping monthly co-pays at $25 for life-saving medications like inhalers and epinephrine, and creating an Essential Benefits Health Insurance Plan to reduce premiums by nearly 20% for Texas families and small businesses.

campaign_platform_points: Jobs & labor: Crowley will grow Wisconsin's economy through local ownership and union labor, expanding his Building Bridges Program statewide to revitalize commercial corridors and create good-paying jobs with strong labor standards.
Healthcare: Crowley will expand mobile health outreach, increase access to addiction treatment, and innovate EMS services across Wisconsin to ensure care reaches people where and when they need it.

Housing: Crowley will build and preserve affordable housing in rural, urban, and suburban communities, cut barriers slowing new construction, and ensure homes are energy-efficient, resilient, and within reach for working families.

Education: Crowley will provide universal early childhood education, make new investments in public schools, and close the special education reimbursement gap to give every child a launchpad to success.

Environment & climate: Crowley will invest in solar power, energy retrofits, and clean infrastructure to create thousands of union jobs statewide, building on his record of cutting Milwaukee County emissions nearly 50%.
Economy & cost of living: Crowley will cap out-of-pocket childcare costs at 7% for all families, include paid family leave, and provide direct support for childcare providers to stabilize the sector.

Transportation: Crowley will close Wisconsin's broadband gap, repair roads, and expand transit where needed, strengthening regional connections between rural communities and economic centers for seniors, workers, and families.

Civil liberties, privacy & surveillance: Crowley will protect voting rights, push for nonpartisan redistricting at every level of government, and strengthen democratic systems to ensure every voice is heard.

campaign_platform_points: Healthcare: Eric Barlow prioritizes rural healthcare as a day-one priority, supporting telehealth expansion, stabilizing rural hospitals, strengthening the healthcare workforce, and reducing regulatory burdens on providers to make care more accessible and affordable.

Economy & cost of living: Barlow supports protecting and enhancing coal, oil, gas, and uranium production, streamlining permitting to keep energy decisions in Wyoming rather than federal bureaucracies, and responsible resource development with respect for private property and water rights.

Government accountability & ethics: Barlow advocates for a small, accountable government that lives within its means through cash-based budgeting, protects individual freedom, respects local authority, and avoids unnecessary interference in people's lives and businesses.

Economy & cost of living: Barlow supports strengthening Wyoming's core industries—minerals, energy, tourism, and agriculture—while encouraging small-business growth, innovation in new technologies and manufacturing, and partnerships to grow the future workforce.

Education: Barlow supports local control and parental involvement in Wyoming schools, keeping education decisions with families and local school boards rather than distant agencies, and expanding vocational programs, trades training, and ag-science pathways for youth.

Environment & climate: Barlow supports keeping Wyoming's public lands in public hands, opposing attempts to wholesale or fire-sale them, and working against federal policies that limit access, undermine multiple use, or ignore local input in managing public lands.

Civil liberties, privacy & surveillance: Barlow defends the Second Amendment and constitutional freedoms, having supported legislation to strengthen concealed carry and sponsored a bill that restored firearms rights to hundreds of Wyoming citizens.

Other: Barlow is firmly pro-life with a consistent legislative record supporting protections for the unborn, and believes supporting life means supporting families through community-based care, maternal health, and resources for women and children.

Education: Romero will push for serious oversight, real consequences, and basic accountability in California's community college system to combat widespread fraud in the application process that steals resources from real students and working people.

Education: Romero will fight to more fully integrate the K-12 system with higher education so that students graduate high school able to read and do basic math, preparing them for college, careers, and life rather than serving as a public works program for adults.

Civil liberties, privacy & surveillance: Romero will hold university administrators and officials accountable to ensure non-discrimination in access to every campus and academic programming, specifically calling out that Jewish students and students of every faith deserve safety, dignity, and equal treatment on campus.

Other: Romero will stand up for women's sports and Title IX, arguing that women deserve a level playing field in athletics rather than excuses, and will advocate for fairness in women's sports policy.

Environment & climate: Romero will restructure and streamline state land and coastal commissions, advocate for fire prevention, smarter land management, and faster rebuilding after disasters, rejecting what she calls a 'Let Them Burn' malfeasance by Sacramento bureaucracy.

Environment & climate: Romero will work with federal partners to safely provide for uncovering untapped energy reserves in California, framing energy development as compatible with environmental protection and community needs.

Economy & cost of living: Romero states a core goal of reducing California's cost of living to restore opportunity, affordability, and what she calls the California Dream, alongside her education reform agenda.

campaign_platform_points: Environment & climate: Proposes a single-payer, public, nonprofit natural disaster insurance system for every Californian, replacing the privately run FAIR Plan. Coverage would be automatic and universal, with premiums tied to mitigation, investment in fire prevention and resilience infrastructure, and requiring worst corporate polluters to pay into the system.

Government accountability & ethics: Will pursue legislation to prohibit insurers from raising premiums, dropping coverage, or refusing renewal for filing a claim or experiencing a no-fault loss. Will require interest payments on delayed claims and immediate full contents payout for total disaster losses.

Economy & cost of living: Will enforce minimum coverage standards as a condition of rate approval, including guaranteed replacement cost for total losses, extended replacement cost up to 50%, ordinance and law coverage up to 25%, requiring consent for reduced coverage, and six months notice before non-renewal or material changes.

Economy & cost of living: Will establish minimum loss ratio standards over rolling three-year periods: 70% for auto insurance and 65% for homeowners insurance, ensuring premium dollars go to paying claims rather than excessive profits or executive compensation.

Economy & cost of living: Long-term goal is to build a public auto insurance option to compete in the market for affordable car insurance. In the short term, will expand the existing low-cost auto insurance program to more working families.

Jobs & labor: Will close the regulatory loophole allowing auto insurers to charge higher rates to blue-collar workers than white-collar workers based on occupation, ending price discrimination in auto insurance pricing.

Healthcare: Will write a plan to guarantee healthcare for every child in California called Medicare for Kids, addressing the roughly 400,000 children who lose Medi-Cal coverage annually due to income changes or paperwork errors.

Government accountability & ethics: Will create a public insurer performance dashboard with company-by-company claims data, a searchable expenditure database, and an annual 'Where Your Premium Goes' report. Will launch market conduct examinations of insurers with elevated complaint rates and coordinate fraud referrals with the Attorney General.

Education: The campaign commits to recruiting and retaining top educators and building a curriculum centered on practical skills to prepare students for success, addressing teacher shortages that strain California classrooms.

Education: The campaign criticizes pandemic-era school closures and mask/vaccine mandates as placing politics over families, arguing these measures set students back years in education and mental health. It pledges to put families' needs first going forward.

Education: The campaign pledges to hold the education system accountable to measurable results rather than political theater, using the Chino Valley model of getting students back in class and prioritizing core subjects as a statewide blueprint.

Parental rights in schools: The campaign criticizes pandemic-era mask and vaccine mandates as heavy-handed measures that ignored families' well-being and set children back years, pledging to prevent similar top-down impositions.

campaign_platform_points: Criminal justice & public safety: Fully fund the Police Department to at least 2,100 officers, increase civilianization of desk jobs, support de-escalation and crisis-response training, strengthen civilian oversight and accountability, and expand visible outreach programs to make streets safer for residents and visitors.

Housing: Build more housing at all income levels, prioritize affordable and workforce housing, make ADUs easier to build, streamline permitting with clear timelines, focus density along transit corridors, and protect rent control and anti-displacement protections alongside new development.

Homelessness: Expand permanent supportive, interim, and sober housing; strengthen behavioral health services and clinically-staffed outreach; advance a balanced approach to open-air drug use combining harm reduction with enforcement; and set transparent benchmarks for measurable outcomes in shelter and housing placements.

Economy & cost of living: Streamline and consolidate the permitting process, reduce unnecessary delays, prioritize first-time, immigrant, and family-owned businesses in ground-floor retail, and provide targeted financial assistance, facade improvement grants, and technical support to help small businesses recover and fill empty storefronts.

Jobs & labor: Fight for good jobs with local hiring, prevailing wages, and strong workforce standards; partner with community colleges for career technical education; raise labor standards and protect union rights; and support growth in both the innovation sector and the care economy including child care and elder care.

Education: Invest in affordable and universal childcare, expand early learning access, strengthen neighborhood public schools with equitable funding, work with City College to expand the Free City College program beyond tuition, and enshrine free City College permanently in the City Charter.

Transportation: Prioritize safer, cleaner, more reliable public transit; expand traffic safety enforcement especially in school zones; prevent SFMTA decisions lacking community buy-in; support biking to reduce congestion; increase parking options; and reopen the Great Highway on weekdays to reduce neighborhood traffic.

Immigration: Ensure the City does not participate in federal immigration raids or share data with ICE; defend Sanctuary City laws; defend DEI policies and access to gender-affirming care; and expand legal defense, know-your-rights education, and culturally competent services for immigrant families.

Supports using reserves as a temporary lifeline and progressive long-term revenue solutions.

Transportation: Supports the progressive parcel tax for Muni and calls for more frequent service, restoring transit lines connecting District 6 to the rest of the city, and creating transit priority lanes to keep buses from getting stuck in traffic.

Environment & climate: Calls for widening sidewalks, removing traffic lanes to slow cars, building safer street crossings, expanding tree canopy to clean air and reduce noise, and investing in residential alleys for children's play, addressing District 6's worst air pollution and highest traffic fatalities.

Jobs & labor: Argues all San Francisco workers must have a right to legal counsel to enforce labor rights, work in safe conditions, and pursue employment claims ignored by the Office of Labor Standards Enforcement, noting employers often find it more profitable to break the law.

Criminal justice & public safety: Demands the Board of Supervisors drop all charges against Trans March and Stud Alley gathering attendees, invest in community-led safety rather than police, and replace police presence at marches with civilian traffic management by SFMTA.

campaign_platform_points: Housing: Supports building housing at every level (affordable, middle-income, supportive, market-rate), rent control, tenant protections, CEQA and historic preservation reform to prevent misuse against new housing, and Mayor Lurie's Family Zoning plan to meet state housing goals.

Criminal justice & public safety: Advocates a holistic public safety approach: expanding and funding mental health crisis response teams, community-based violence prevention, substance use treatment, and ensuring first responders (police, firefighters, 311) have adequate resources and capacity.

Economy & cost of living: Will cut red tape and streamline permitting for small businesses, continue the first-year-free program, grow neighborhood anchoring and legacy business programs, and invest in early childhood education and public schools so working families can stay in San Francisco.

Immigration: Committed to defending San Francisco's Sanctuary City status, keeping ICE out of the city, strengthening immigrant legal defense and rapid response networks, supporting notification systems for undocumented residents, and protecting workers from retaliation tied to immigration status.

Israel / Palestine: Describes Israel's actions in Gaza as genocide, supports a permanent ceasefire, would have voted for the 2024 Board of Supervisors ceasefire resolution, rejects AIPAC money, and opposes sending or funding weapons for Israel.

Other: Will protect LGBTQ+ organizations from federal funding cuts via bridge funding, champion HIV/AIDS prevention and long-term survivor services, fully fund the Office of Transgender Initiatives, invest in the Castro LGBTQ Cultural District, and address hate crimes against LGBTQ+ people.

Transportation: Supports Vision Zero, expanding protected bike lanes and slow streets networks, traffic calming (bulbouts, raised crosswalks, lower speed limits), speed cameras on chronic speeding corridors, and late-night transit for workers and nightlife patrons.

Jobs & labor: Will strengthen union protections in healthcare, hospitality, and public sectors, advance living wages and fair contracts, ensure new housing construction creates good jobs with prevailing wages, and protect immigrant workers from ICE raids.

campaign_platform_points: Housing: Introduce social housing legislation (permanently affordable, mixed-income, city-owned) on day one. Opposed reducing inclusionary housing from 15% to 5%. Supports Prop I (Affordable Housing Guarantee Act) and Prop C (Housing Trust Fund through 2058). Focus on building 17,000 approved units and creating permanent community-owned affordable housing.

Criminal justice & public safety: Opposes expanding Flock surveillance cameras as a mass surveillance threat. Supports community policing, well-lit streets, violence prevention, and Street Crisis Response Team investment. For open drug use, follows four pillars: prevention, treatment, harm reduction, and enforcement. Criticizes RESET center spending as not real treatment.

Transportation: Extend free Muni for youth beyond age 19 through age 25, pending SFMTA fiscal analysis and funding plan. Supports Prop H and the Regional Transit Measure to save Muni service. Frames transit access as essential for young adults to reach school, work, and medical appointments.

Economy & cost of living: Proposes 'Vacant to Vibrant' program extending city support for empty storefronts from three months to two years, paired with commercial rent stabilization. Supports cutting fees to help small businesses thrive and making big corporations pay their fair share. Expands these measures to the Castro for LGBTQ+-owned ventures.

Government accountability & ethics: Opposes Mayor's 'Clean Up City Hall' measures that would raise the ballot initiative signature threshold and expand mayoral power over hiring and firing department heads. Commits to protecting essential checks and balances in City Hall and not being a rubber stamp for the Mayor.

Education: Champions Prop 13 reform to bring $1.1 billion back to schools and local government in San Francisco. Advocates for greater Board of Supervisors collaboration with the school board and state delegation. Argues basic funding for SFUSD and CCSF shouldn't require parcel taxes or bond measures every cycle.

Environment & climate: Calls for a coordinated wildfire mitigation plan for Glen Canyon: clear dangerous brush, thin and maintain eucalyptus trees, remove sick trees, keep evacuation routes open, and coordinate Rec and Park, Public Works, Fire Department, and PUC. Opposes clear-cutting due to landslide risk.

Healthcare: Opposes cuts to services for people living with HIV/AIDS, calling them life-saving. Notes the Mayor attempted deep cuts that were reversed through community organizing. Commits to not cutting services for this community, framing it as a moral obligation in the richest city in the world.

campaign_platform_points: Housing: The campaign pledges to close the gap between housing approvals and actual construction by enforcing permitting timelines with automatic escalation, extending expiring fee reductions, and building local financing tools independent of federal dollars. Also pushes for a public housing pipeline tracker and visitability standards in all new residential construction.

Criminal justice & public safety: The campaign calls for auditing and capping SFPD overtime spending, expanding the Street Crisis Response Team for non-criminal 911 calls, and implementing coordinated block-level investments in lighting and programming. Also demands proper classification of hate crimes in the Castro and dedicated investigation capacity.

Homelessness: The campaign prioritizes prevention over shelter, proposing expanded rapid re-housing and targeted rental assistance for cost-burdened households. It also calls for requiring outreach teams to connect people to available services before encampment clearances, and for convening a community process to identify a D8 shelter site.

Transportation: The campaign supports funding Muni through November ballot measures to avoid a $307 million fiscal cliff, demands route-level on-time performance data be published alongside headway data, and requires an equity analysis before any route elimination serving transit-dependent populations.

Education: The campaign proposes requiring new residential and mixed-use developments on transit corridors to include ground-floor spaces built to childcare licensing specs, opening empty rec center rooms for licensed providers, and cutting ELFA voucher enrollment wait from twelve months to ninety days.

Economy & cost of living: The campaign pledges to shift commercial permitting from a 'no, unless' to 'yes, if' posture, pre-clear commercial kitchen permits, enforce the existing vacancy tax with escalating rates for chronic vacancies, and opt into California's home kitchen law for microenterprise operators.

Civil liberties, privacy & surveillance: The campaign supports the city's camera network but demands guardrails including a federal data-sharing prohibition barring sharing with ICE, DHS, or FBI without a warrant, an independent annual bias audit of camera deployment, and reinstating the governance framework removed by Prop E.

Environment & climate: The campaign calls for a pre-positioned wildfire smoke response plan including air purifier distribution, certified clean-air shelters at rec centers and libraries, and automatic notifications at hazardous AQI levels. It also pushes to restore the Environment Department's core capacity after an 80% budget cut.

campaign_platform_points: Housing: Build the 20,000-unit pipeline at Pier 70, Power Station, India Basin, Shipyard, and Candlestick; defend rent control; expand Certificate of Preference and down-payment assistance; streamline permitting; legalize infill density; rebuild public housing into mixed-income communities without displacing residents.

Homelessness: Expand shelters, supportive and drug-free housing, mental health and substance use treatment beds, and sober living with wraparound services. Fix funding rules so public dollars can flow to recovery housing. Support the One City Shelter Act for fair distribution across all districts.

Criminal justice & public safety: Fill the roughly 500-officer police shortage with lateral bonuses and faster background checks; restore beat cops to corridors; fund violence prevention for at-risk youth; properly resource Bayview Station; ensure police accountability with meaningful civilian oversight.

Environment & climate: Deliver independent community-supervised re-testing of the entire Hunters Point Shipyard site; mandate no building on contaminated parcels until verified safe; push for no-cost electrification retrofits for legacy homeowners; invest in parks, tree canopy, and clean air monitoring from Candlestick to India Basin.

Transportation: Fix the T Third with signal priority and better stops; bring Caltrain downtown; deliver ferry service from Mission Bay, Dogpatch, and the Shipyard; replace the Islais Creek Bridge properly; build the Blue Greenway and Bayview Community Pathway for safe biking.

Jobs & labor: Write local hiring and workforce development into every major project; close the talent gap with union apprenticeships and neighborhood training; preserve industrial space for manufacturing and life sciences; extend the First Year Free business program; support project labor agreements on major developments.

Education: Launch a High School-to-Career Pathway Program connecting students to paid apprenticeships, credentials, and careers in high-demand industries including tech, construction, healthcare, and life sciences. Build a citywide partnership among SFUSD, City College, UCSF, USF, unions, and employers.

Civil liberties, privacy & surveillance: Sanctuary City policy is non-negotiable with no city cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. Defend reproductive and gender-affirming care from federal attack. Protect schools, clinics, and houses of worship as safe spaces. Strengthen hate crime reporting and cross-community coalitions.

campaign_platform_points: Housing: Community-centered housing development, preservation, and rehabilitation using neighborhood plans that incorporate community input, long-term needs, and space for small businesses. Fight displacement of families and small businesses. Push for family-friendly units and affordable housing in new developments.

Criminal justice & public safety: Implement proven crime reduction tactics like community policing and neighborhood-based foot patrols in District 10. Push for community enrichment programs including summer youth jobs and after-school programs. Work with families, merchants, and neighborhood groups on streetscaping and safe public parks.

Transportation: Expand transit connections, walking and biking paths, and build the long-delayed Bayview CalTrain Station. Advocate for safe bicycle lanes throughout the district. Support new growth with new transit infrastructure to connect residents to the rest of San Francisco.

Economy & cost of living: Strengthen local merchant corridors including Third Street, Leland, and 17th Street through streetscaping, community policing, festivals, and consistent street cleaning. Support local small businesses and commercial corridors as the foundation for walkable, liveable communities.

Jobs & labor: Center new economic plans on affordable housing so jobs don't displace residents. Create job opportunities through local recruitment, job training with City College, mentorship and internship programs for young people, and dedicated spaces for legacy small businesses and community organizations.

Environment & climate: Advocate for state and federal oversight and funding for the Hunters Point shipyard cleanup to ensure safe, verifiable remediation results. Address environmental racism affecting Black San Franciscans in the district who face higher mortality rates due to contamination.

Homelessness: Advocate for supportive housing, shelters, and behavioral health facilities for unhoused residents in District 10. Push for city-wide comprehensive solutions so every part of San Francisco shares responsibility for addressing the homelessness crisis on the streets.

Other: Support creative fiscal solutions including a public bank and enhanced infrastructure finance districts to ensure projects can start when ready. Engage all stakeholders and refuse to give up until roadblocks to housing, parks, and commercial corridor improvements are removed.

campaign_platform_points: Other: The campaign supports converting the former Golden Gate Fields site into a waterfront park, citing Measure C zoning, the 2010 Voices to Visions project, and a $125 million state investment. They commit to keeping Albany's community at the table with the State, Berkeley, and East Bay Regional Parks on amenities and decisions.

Economy & cost of living: The campaign supports new revenue measures to fund city services (EMS, sidewalks, storm drain) while ensuring tax structures are progressive with rebates or exemptions for lower-income households. They oppose cutting staff and services as an alternative to funding.

Civil liberties, privacy & surveillance: The campaign supports ending the city's contract with the ALPR camera vendor and removing all automated license plate reader cameras from Albany, citing the company's repeated betrayal of public trust as revealed in national news.

Criminal justice & public safety: The campaign wants to restore an unarmed crisis response team to Albany, noting that the previous provider could no longer continue service. They believe some residents are better served by non-uniformed, non-armed responders alongside the police department's deescalation focus.

Housing: The campaign supports building more housing in Albany by funding new 100% affordable projects, opening the zoning code to allow more building, and providing services and protections to help residents stay housed or regain safe, stable, affordable housing. They cite the Verana Hill project and tenant eviction protections as past actions.

Transportation: The campaign supports walkable, bikeable streets, the Complete Streets plan, bulbouts, bicycle infrastructure, and the recently approved Active Transportation Plan. They also support engaging with the regional transit network and right-sizing public transit options to community needs.

Environment & climate: The campaign supports reducing Albany's emissions through Ava Community Energy's cleaner energy mix, e-bike subsidies, electric cooking retrofits, heat pump rebates, and a pilot program to electrify an entire city block. They aim to make Albany's energy cleaner and return more of residents' bills locally.

Other: The campaign emphasizes regional cooperation among neighboring cities to offset federal grant revocations and resource losses under the current administration, arguing that standing together ensures Albany has the resources it needs for local services.

campaign_platform_points: Criminal justice & public safety: Committed to maintaining rapid police and fire response times, continuing neighborhood patrols, keeping school campuses safe, enforcing weed abatement for fire prevention, expanding community outreach programs including C.A.R.E. Teams, and ensuring equitable service through ongoing training assessments.

Housing: Delivered 508 new housing units including 130 affordable units, met and exceeded state housing goals while preserving neighborhood character, opened Firehouse Square with 66 affordable units downtown, and adopted a housing preference policy for San Mateo County residents and displaced households.

Transportation: Repaired dozens of streets through the Street Improvement Program, repaved Ralston Avenue, upgraded sewer infrastructure, and authorized the Belmont Village Bike and Pedestrian Project to create new bike lanes, crossings, and routes beginning in Downtown Belmont.

Other: Approved a 15-year Parks, Recreation, and Open Space Master Plan for park maintenance and improvement, building a modern Belmont Community Center, and maintaining parks, trails, and open spaces while ensuring safety for hikers and all users.

Economy & cost of living: Began developing the Harbor Industrial Area Specific Plan to explore annexation for increased employment and tax revenue, leading discussions with Stanford on the Notre Dame de Namur campus acquisition, and revitalizing vacant downtown parcels through mixed-use development.

Environment & climate: Working to further climate action goals in response to the threat of climate change, including completing a rehabilitation of Belmont's storm and sanitation infrastructure in 2023 to improve resilience.

Other: Increased city-sponsored programming and events for all residents, including summer Camp SOAR, Inclusion Camp for children with disabilities, and celebrations of cultural diversity such as Pride Month, Diwali, Lunar New Year, and Dr. King poetry contests.

Government accountability & ethics: Stated that the move to district-based council elections is not appropriate for Belmont, reflecting the city leadership's and residents' preference for the existing at-large election system for council members.

state.office: At large Rent Stabilization Board Commissioner
campaign_platform_points: Housing: The campaign's central mission is to stabilize rent increases, protect and preserve rent-controlled and affordable housing in Berkeley, and ensure safe and healthy homes for all residents.
Housing: Avery Arbaugh calls on UC Berkeley to take responsibility for the student housing crisis and pledges to represent and protect students and young renters on the Rent Board.
Housing: The campaign commits to ensuring that senior renters have accessible and affordable housing, addressing the specific needs of older tenants in Berkeley's rental market.

Jobs & labor: Avery Arbaugh supports empowering tenants to form unions and organize collectively to negotiate better living conditions, building on her work under Berkeley's Tenant Protection and Right to Organize Act.
Housing: The campaign pledges to provide legal support to tenants who need assistance navigating housing disputes, repairs, and rent stabilization issues before the Rent Board.

Economy & cost of living: Avery Arbaugh proposes that the Rent Board factor in annual Cost-of-Living Adjustments to SSI and SSDI benefits when setting rent stabilization limits for fixed-income tenants.
Housing: The campaign supports enshrining the Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act in Berkeley law and passing a strong Tenant Bill of Rights to codify and expand tenant protections.

Government accountability & ethics: Avery Arbaugh pledges to keep the Rent Board free from corporate influence, specifically opposing efforts by the BPOA and other corporate entities to weaken tenant protections, and will not accept money from corporations, fossil fuels, or military contractors.

campaign_platform_points: Housing: Support new housing at all income levels including subsidized, supportive, and market-rate units. Advocate strong tenant protections, encourage missing-middle and ADU housing, support zoning changes for affordable-by-design homes, and prioritize housing near transit.

Homelessness: Restore funding for existing programs like the Hope Center and RV buyback. Pass an ordinance banning unauthorized encampments. Pursue regional solutions through Alameda County. Fund permanent supportive housing and an inter-jurisdictional RV site.

Transportation: Ensure Measure FF's $270 million is spent effectively on street repairs and safety. Prioritize accessibility for pedestrians, cyclists, and people with disabilities. Fix broken sidewalks, support District 1's Equity Zone for priority paving, and add street trees.

Criminal justice & public safety: Provide police resources for violent crime response and prevention. Support Police Accountability Board oversight. Oppose Flock surveillance technology. Support non-sworn first responders, community policing, and restore funding for a clinician-staffed non-transport response unit.

Government accountability & ethics: Provide rigorous budget oversight aligned with voter intent. Streamline permitting for housing and small businesses. Invest in operational efficiency like modernizing software systems. Prioritize timely constituent services and responsive communication with residents.

Environment & climate: Plant more street trees especially in flatlands. Keep parks clean and maintained. Protect the shoreline and invest in Berkeley Marina for sea level rise. Convert Golden Gate Fields into a public park with wetland habitat restoration and bay access.

Government accountability & ethics: Kromer advocates faster, more predictable permit processes with published median decision times by permit type. Criminal justice & public safety: Kromer calls for competent public safety and well-maintained parks in District 1 (Ohlone, Cedar Rose, James Kenney, North Waterfront), with a published maintenance schedule and park condition reports kept current to ensure shared spaces remain safe and usable.

Jobs & labor: Kromer supports protecting West Berkeley's industrial-arts economy by keeping land zoned for making, putting the permit process on the public record with steps, costs, and waits, and tracking whether makers remain year over year.

Housing: On corridor upzoning, Kromer supports design standards (shadow, wind, setbacks, street trees) on San Pablo before applications arrive, but would vote no on added heights on Solano and College where no state floor applies, with tenant and small-business protections in the ordinance text.

campaign_platform_points: Housing: Supports building new housing of all types—affordable, subsidized, cooperative, land trust, and market-rate affordable-by-design—for students, seniors, and families. Also supports universal tenant protections, tenant unions, TOPA pathways to ownership, and the Small Sites program for affordable family housing.

Homelessness: Treats homelessness as a public health emergency rather than a criminal issue. Supports opening an emergency Alternative Sites shelter with running water, sanitation, and wrap-around services; investing in Housing First programs; avoiding punitive citations and arrests; and no further cuts to behavioral health programs.

Civil liberties, privacy & surveillance: Calls for canceling Berkeley's Flock automated license plate reader contract, arguing it has a clear pattern of abuse and misuse that no municipal privacy policy can remedy. Advocates switching to ALPR systems that do not threaten civil liberties and eliminating mass surveillance in the city.

Criminal justice & public safety: Advocates keeping fire and police budgets solvent through revenue measures, investing in crime prevention through urban lighting, afterschool programming, and street diversion, hiring mental health responders and civilian enforcement, respecting the Police Accountability Board, and maintaining progressive use-of-force policies.

Economy & cost of living: Committed to investing in small businesses by reducing vacant storefronts, cutting permitting wait times and processing fees, expanding open space and parklets, and supporting 'Mom and Pop' landlords as partners in addressing the housing shortage while keeping commercial spaces vibrant.

Transportation: Supports building street infrastructure designed for a future with more cyclists, more transit, and denser communities. Backs aligning and implementing Berkeley's current streets studies to create safe streets for all residents.

Government accountability & ethics: Commits to keeping city workers and unions involved in every budget step, planning for long-term pension liabilities and deferred maintenance, and engaging the community through participatory budgeting models where neighbors caucus and negotiate priorities with real-world constraints.

Immigration: Supports maintaining and expanding Berkeley's sanctuary city protections, tenant rights, and labor protections for immigrant and marginalized communities. Frames opposition to ICE and federal immigration enforcement as a core campaign priority.

campaign_platform_points: Housing: The campaign calls for more housing production combined with tenant protections, preservation of existing lower-cost housing, permanently affordable homes, and preventing displacement. New development should contribute to neighborhood infrastructure and quality of life.

Other: The campaign treats parks, sidewalks, public restrooms, trees, and gathering spaces as essential civic infrastructure. It calls for maintaining and improving public spaces, expanding amenities, and restoring People's Park as public land and ecological space.

Government accountability & ethics: The campaign demands transparent, measurable city government with regular public updates, clear timelines, community check-ins on major projects, and tracking of outcomes so residents can distinguish what was requested, approved, funded, delivered, and maintained.

Environment & climate: The campaign calls for practical climate resilience improvements including upgrading stormwater and street infrastructure, expanding shade and cooling, supporting clean energy and efficient buildings, improving sidewalks, and prioritizing investments in high-use areas like Southside.

Criminal justice & public safety: The campaign argues public safety should focus on prevention rather than reaction, investing in clean streets, lighting, mental health services, crisis response connected to care, pedestrian safety, and building public trust through transparency and accountability.

Economy & cost of living: The campaign supports reducing bureaucratic barriers for small businesses, supporting local hiring, maintaining clean and accessible commercial corridors, and strengthening connections between economic activity, transit, housing, and public space planning.

Government accountability & ethics: The campaign insists that UC Berkeley, developers, and City Hall should bear the cost of services, safety, transit, and maintenance that their growth and expansion require, rather than shifting those costs onto existing residents.

Housing: The plan calls for earlier city assistance when a renter receives an eviction notice, a social-housing and preservation partnership, clearer housing-delivery procedures, stronger public and community ownership, and public reporting throughout the housing process.

campaign_platform_points: Housing: Advocates a 'tailored zoning' approach for Elmwood that limits rezoning to three specific underutilized parking-lot sites (7-11, Wells Fargo lot, Post Office parcel) to meet state housing mandates while protecting the pedestrian-oriented retail fabric and local shops.

Civil liberties, privacy & surveillance: Supports automated license plate readers as a public-safety tool but insists on strict City data controls, regular auditing, high vendor standards, and contract escape clauses allowing the City to cancel at any time without penalty.

Other: Acknowledges strong community desire to reopen Willard Pool but notes the City has few tools since BUSD owns the property. Would welcome a citizen's initiative to fund reopening or purchase of the site.

Housing: Brokered a Council compromise on middle housing to allow medium-density, naturally affordable homes in neighborhoods previously zoned exclusively for single-family, finding a middle path between competing proposals.

Transportation: Championed low-cost 'quick build' safety improvements on Claremont Avenue to reduce speeding and improve safety for pedestrians, cyclists, and drivers, as a precursor to longer-term flood-control-related upgrades.

Transportation: Actively lobbied state legislators to include Berkeley in pilot programs for automated speed-enforcement cameras, calling them a no-brainer for street safety, and continues to advocate for their expansion.

Transportation: Initiated a staff study of four-way stop sign improvements at key intersections to slow traffic, increase safety, and pursue newer, more flexible installation standards following a series of serious accidents.

Housing: Fights for regulatory fairness and flexibility for small mom-and-pop landlords who own duplexes or ADUs and live on-site with tenants, resisting onerous requirements that could force them to keep problematic tenants long-term.

Supports streamlined permitting for homeowners, open housing data, Community Benefit Programs, historic district protection, and mixed-income development to prevent income segregation.

Transportation: Calls for real traffic safety on Claremont Avenue including a proper signal at the school zone, sustained speed enforcement, dedicated cyclist lanes, utility undergrounding, street lighting upgrades, and data-driven traffic analysis ahead of the underground bypass project.

Government accountability & ethics: Wants a council representative who collaborates with UC Berkeley while defending District 8 residents. Cites concerns about stadium debt, parking congestion on Bancroft Way, lack of joint housing planning with admissions growth, and the university's low settlement payments relative to peer institutions.

campaign_platform_points: Transportation: Stevenson prioritizes pedestrian and bicyclist street safety and commits to engaging with major regional transportation projects, including the Caltrain grade separation at Broadway and the US-101/Peninsula Avenue interchange, to influence their outcomes for District 5 and Burlingame.

Environment & climate: Stevenson wants Burlingame to lead Bay Area climate initiatives, specifically protecting the bay front ecosystem, improving public transit to reduce car dependence, adopting green-focused building codes, and pursuing alternative energy for city operations.

Housing: Stevenson calls for a holistic approach to affordability, including increasing the supply of both rental and entry-level homeownership units and developing creative solutions to prevent displacement of residents already living in established apartments.

Other: Stevenson advocates incorporating age-friendly design and planning into all land use, development, transportation, safety, and recreational decisions, citing the projected growth of the 60-plus population in the Bay Area from 19% in 2020 to 30% by 2030.

Other: Stevenson supports expanding recreational programs for adults, teens, and youth, adding recreational facilities, and ensuring adequate shared public space is included in all commercial development planning.

Economy & cost of living: Stevenson commits to continuing support for local businesses as a source of employment and community character, while promoting a diversity of service, product, and experience options for all residents in downtown districts.

Education: Stevenson emphasizes that strong public and private schools are foundational to the city and pledges to foster collaboration and coordination between the city government and educational leaders, drawing on his prior roles in school PTA and education foundation leadership.

campaign_platform_points: Economy & cost of living: Supports Measure M (1% sales tax increase) as a near-term stop-gap but stresses it is not a stable revenue source. Calls for disciplined budgeting, maintaining healthy reserves, avoiding unnecessary debt, and seeking additional sustainable revenue sources for the city's long-term financial future.

Other: Prioritizes clearing the backlog of deferred maintenance on streets, sidewalks, and trails. Commits to ensuring infrastructure projects do not stall due to administrative gaps or staffing continuity problems, and to making the most of existing federal and state grant funds.

Housing: Acknowledks valid concerns about traffic and infrastructure strain but argues Clayton should not leave housing decisions to the state. Calls for the city to lead the conversation by collaborating with neighboring cities and the County to develop housing and transportation solutions while preserving local character.

Criminal justice & public safety: Commits to keeping Clayton among California's safest communities by actively supporting local law enforcement, improving emergency preparedness, and promoting neighborhood safety programs.

Government accountability & ethics: Pledges to bring back civility, accountability, and accessibility to City Council. Commits to open access to all proceedings and voting records, full ownership of council decisions, and honest communication without political spin.

Transportation: Supports common-sense e-bike education, better public communication of rules, and thoughtful enforcement to protect riders, pedestrians, and drivers. Calls for updating outdated local bicycle and e-bike licensing rules to align with evolving state safety laws.

Other: Supports renewal of the Landscape Maintenance District (Measure N) as a firm funding source for trails, open space, roadside landscaping, and weed abatement. Argues investing in public spaces is both beautification and a practical risk management strategy.

Other: Calls for putting the city-managed Concerts in the Grove series back on a self-sustaining footing by reviewing unnecessary spending since 2023, restoring the Patron Sponsor program, and considering a return to volunteer management for city-sponsored events.

campaign_platform_points: Transportation: The campaign prioritizes a steady multi-year repaving program across major arterials and residential streets in the district, and supports interconnected traffic signals along major corridors to ease congestion and keep traffic moving.

Criminal justice & public safety: The campaign supports full police staffing, the Real Time Intelligence Center (drones, cameras, real-time crime analysis), body-worn cameras for transparency, and recruitment/retention programs to rebuild the department after the pandemic.

Homelessness: The campaign backs a dedicated full-time CORE outreach team, partnerships with organizations like Hope Solutions and Caminar for rapid rehousing and mental-health support, and conversion of the former Valley Motel into permanent supportive housing.

Housing: The campaign supports new affordable housing downtown near BART, including 181 all-affordable apartments at Blue Oak Square and roughly 400 units for seniors, veterans, and people with disabilities, plus a First-Time Homebuyer Program offering down-payment assistance.

Environment & climate: The campaign supports park improvements including water quality and habitat restoration at Newhall Community Park, community events at Todos Santos Plaza, and ensuring roughly 2,500 acres of the former Naval Weapons Station become a new East Bay Regional Park District park.

Other: The campaign supports senior mobility programs (Concord Go!, GoGo Concord), Senior Center programming, youth camps, swim lessons, and a Youth Scholarship Program providing funding so income-eligible children can participate in recreation programs regardless of family finances.

Economy & cost of living: The campaign supports balanced budgets and a Rainy Day Fund, and voted to place Measure O on the ballot to modernize Concord's outdated business-license tax into a simpler, fairer system generating locally controlled funding for road maintenance and emergency response.

Other: The campaign supports responsible reuse of the former Concord Naval Weapons Station with Brookfield as master developer, a 100-yard buffer between new development and existing homes, and community involvement in the planning process.

campaign_platform_points: Housing: Expand housing supply and protect tenants from displacement to keep Daly City affordable and stable. The campaign highlights passing K-12 educator housing and large mixed-income developments as past achievements and frames housing equity as a central priority.

Government accountability & ethics: Expand multilingual access, neighborhood outreach, and meaningful participation opportunities so working-class families, immigrants, youth, and seniors have real power in shaping local government decisions. Emphasizes transparent, community-led decisions and accessible services.

Jobs & labor: Support local small businesses, good union jobs, fair wages, and apprenticeship pathways connecting young people, immigrants, and working families to lasting careers. Public development funding should yield local hiring, safe workplaces, and community benefits.

Environment & climate: Commit to a greener and healthier community through clean energy, green spaces, and collaboration with community organizations and regional political bodies to address environmental challenges for future generations.

Criminal justice & public safety: Public safety should be rooted in care, prevention, and community connection rather than fear or punishment. Supports mental-health resources, youth opportunities, safer streets, and neighborhood-based solutions that prevent harm before it occurs.

Other: Create leadership infrastructures and mentorship programs so young people become politically engaged and step into leadership roles. The campaign frames youth civic engagement as vital to the future of the country and the city.

Healthcare: Advocate for expanded mental-health support, first-aid training, and cultural events that strengthen community belonging and combat loneliness. Mental-health care is positioned as a core public service alongside housing and economic opportunity.

Immigration: The campaign pledges a Daly City where immigrants can stay, participate, and thrive alongside working families, youth, and seniors. A video titled 'Sanctuary For All' signals a pro-sanctuary stance, and multilingual engagement is a stated priority.

Economy & cost of living: Kashef emphasizes a practical, solutions-oriented approach focused on fiscal responsibility, community resilience, and broader sustainability in his governance and policy decisions for Dublin.

campaign_platform_points: Housing: Dublin grew 62% in a decade and growth must match infrastructure. Shivraj commits to requiring binding infrastructure-first development agreements for mega-projects, expanding community input periods, and auditing cumulative traffic impacts before new approvals.

Criminal justice & public safety: Crime concerns have nearly doubled since 2019. Shivraj commits to police staffing benchmarks tied to population milestones, funding a mental health co-responder program pairing counselors with officers for crisis calls, and expanding wildfire and earthquake emergency preparedness.

Transportation: Shivraj will fight to accelerate the long-overdue 1.5-mile Dublin Boulevard Extension from Fallon Road to North Canyons Parkway, create a BART last-mile shuttle program connecting neighborhoods to stations, and require cumulative traffic analysis for projects over 100 units.

Other: Dublin must invest in all generations: expand subsidized childcare slots and partner with employers to bring care closer to where families live, increase senior transportation options, and fund youth after-school and recreation programs to close funding gaps.

Government accountability & ethics: Rapid development generates millions in developer fees. Shivraj commits to launching a public-facing open budget dashboard, requiring annual independent fiscal audits, and mandating transparent developer fee tracking and public reporting from collection to expenditure.

Education: DUSD enrollment rose 92% in a decade and 700 teachers struck in March 2026. Shivraj commits to requiring school impact assessments for every major development, strengthening joint-use agreements between the city and DUSD, and advocating for fair developer fee allocation to school infrastructure.

Housing: Growth must match infrastructure. Every major development project should require binding infrastructure-first agreements, extended community input periods, and cumulative traffic impact analysis before approval. Residents deserve a seat at the table before projects are greenlit.

Transportation: Accelerate the long-overdue Dublin Boulevard Extension (1.5-mile link from Fallon Road to North Canyons Parkway). Create a BART last-mile shuttle program connecting neighborhoods to stations. Require cumulative traffic impact analysis for all residential projects over 100 units.

Transportation: The campaign pledges to calm neighborhood traffic to make streets safer for children, families, and seniors across all neighborhoods in East Palo Alto.
Education: The candidate commits to investing in youth and parks by expanding safe, enriching recreational and educational opportunities for the next generation in East Palo Alto.

Criminal justice & public safety: The campaign frames public safety as a non-partisan issue focused on protecting children, supporting families, and ensuring every resident feels safe on their own street.

state.endorsement_evidence_context: For this rubric, directional CAIR Action / Vote for Peace recommendations, including Ally or Opposed, are concrete stance evidence even without a direct candidate quotation. Preserve their stated tier, phase and source qualifications.

CAIR Action.relevance: Recommendations consider civil rights and foreign policy, including Gaza/ceasefire positions. Preferred is not full endorsement; preserve the recorded tier and joint status.

Vote for Peace.relevance: Evaluates human rights and war-lobby/AIPAC funding, also considering viability. Preserve Ally/Neutral/Opposed; inclusion alone is not endorsement or proof of a specific policy.

pro_palestine_score.instructions: What grade should we give the candidate wrt how pro-Palestine and anti-Israel they are?
criteria: Shields Israel and a strong defender of Israel or has endorsements from Hindutva or Zionist organizations (other than JStreetPAC; Zionist organizations explicitly include California Jewish Democrats, the renamed Democrats for Israel California, and its 'Strong Support' tier counts double against the candidate)

Israel-centric framing with sympathy for Palestinians or equates being anti-zionism or anti-Israel with anti-semitism / supports the IHRA definition of anti-semitism or bills like AB-715 in CA that censor criticism of Israel, or is opposed by any anti-Zionist org like TrackAIPAC or Vote For Peace
Condemns humanitarian harm only without fully blaming Israel or only blaming Netanahu or is a liberal zionist and refuses to say a clear Yes it's a genocide when explicitly asked
Condemns Israel for doing serious war crimes and condemns settler violence in the West Bank, but stop short of calling for ending US aid to Israel or endorsed by JStreet

Explicitly affirms it to be a 'genocide' but leaves room for a reset of Israel-US relations by blaming Netanyahu and the current government only. They are against aid to Israel but they still insist on allowing sales to Israel. They are a champion for getting US out of wars in the middle east. Preferred by CAIR Action.

Openly against the genocide and Israeli military assistance / endorsed by Track AIPAC or CAIR Action (at endorsement level rather than just preferred level) or Vote for Peace / opposed by UDP. An early advocate for calling for a ceasefire in Gaza.  Or we know they are part of the Muslim community, or has personally been a strong champion for our cause such as leading / introducing a ceasefire resolution. Or are openly and explicitly anti-zionist and strong supporters of BDS against Israel. They oppose the US doing things on behalf of Israel. An endorsement from a pro-Palestine organization (CAIR Action, Vote for Peace, Track AIPAC, BAMC) is never by itself sufficient for this top band: a candidate who has said or done nothing personally caps at the band below, and if the same candidate also carries a California Jewish Democrats (ex-DFI) endorsement the two net down to the middle bands (its 'Support' tier nets to the middle, 'Strong Support' further).

campaign_platform_points: Housing: The campaign pledges to champion affordable housing as a core priority for East Palo Alto residents, positioning it as the first of several key issues the candidate will advance on the City Council.

Environment & climate: The campaign commits to environmental justice as a central platform issue, signaling a focus on equitable environmental outcomes and climate-related policy for East Palo Alto communities.

Other: The campaign states a commitment to responsible development, indicating the candidate will advocate for development policies that balance growth with community needs and environmental considerations in East Palo Alto.

Economy & cost of living: The campaign pledges to strengthen local and small businesses in East Palo Alto, framing economic support for neighborhood enterprises as a key priority for residents' quality of life.

Criminal justice & public safety: The campaign identifies community safety as one of its core issue areas, inviting residents passionate about public safety to join the effort to improve conditions in East Palo Alto.

campaign_platform_points: Government accountability & ethics: Jawili pledges to increase transparency in city council decision-making, offer one-on-one office hours, commission resident surveys, meet regularly with community group liaisons, and communicate in plain language across multiple platforms to rebuild trust between residents and city leadership.

Government accountability & ethics: Jawili calls for a clear long-term plan for El Cerrito's pension obligations with understandable public reporting and realistic assumptions, ensuring commitments to city workers don't crowd out services residents depend on today.

Environment & climate: Jawili prioritizes disaster preparedness for wildfire, earthquakes, extreme heat, flooding, and power outages, wanting the city to practice evacuation and communication plans, find gaps before emergencies, and coordinate with neighboring cities and utilities.

Criminal justice & public safety: The campaign commits to responsive police and fire services, emergency preparedness, cybersecurity resilience, and treating public safety as a foundational responsibility of city government.

Transportation: Art opposes reducing Foster City Boulevard from two travel lanes to one, warning it would worsen existing traffic backups approaching Highway 92, while still supporting bike and pedestrian safety improvements.

campaign_platform_points: Economy & cost of living: Phoebe Shin Venkat commits to addressing Foster City's $4 million budget deficit and ongoing structural deficits by working with local, regional, and state agencies, and by collaborating with city staff to create new or deepen existing revenue streams.

campaign_platform_points: Homelessness: Kimberlin advocates for collaborative, practical homelessness solutions tailored to Fremont rather than a one-size-fits-all approach. She voted against the 2025 camping ordinance, successfully pushed to remove its 'aiding and abetting' clause to protect nonprofits, and created a Community Action Forum on Homelessness to sustain cross-jurisdictional coordination.

Economy & cost of living: A top stated priority is supporting small businesses and nonprofits in Fremont by leading local businesses, connecting them with resources, and championing education and support for Tri-City nonprofits through her co-founding of the Tri-City Nonprofit Coalition and leadership of the Fremont Education Foundation.

Criminal justice & public safety: The campaign identifies public safety as a core area of focus alongside smart growth and social/economic development, emphasizing a collaborative approach with City, County, and community members rather than a single-policy stance.

Government accountability & ethics: Kimberlin frames her entire campaign around bringing accessibility, transparency, and integrity to Fremont City Council, positioning herself as an accessible and transparent leader who ensures every resident feels heard, valued, and represented.

Housing: The campaign states she has promoted affordable housing actions in partnership with small businesses and City staff, and her homelessness work includes studying models like Palo Alto Affordable Housing and Lifeline Housing tiny-home units as potential strategies for Fremont.

Jobs & labor: Kimberlin pledges to work collaboratively with residents to bring jobs to Fremont and grow the community, citing her role managing a $3+ million budget that brings resources to small businesses and nonprofits as evidence of her economic-development track record.

campaign_platform_points: Criminal justice & public safety: Supports public safety as a fundamental responsibility, clean neighborhoods, well-maintained parks, streets, and sidewalks, with preventive maintenance over delayed repairs and success measured by everyday resident experience rather than statistics alone.

Homelessness: Advocates practical approaches to homelessness that balance compassion with community responsibility, while also considering regional cooperation, mental health, housing, and program effectiveness rather than viewing the issue through a single lens.

Housing: Supports smart growth that balances new housing development with supporting infrastructure, protects neighborhood livability, considers long-term community impacts, and plans for future generations while encouraging economic opportunity.

Economy & cost of living: Committed to responsible financial stewardship: careful budgeting, transparency in how public funds are used, measurable outcomes from investments, long-term fiscal sustainability, and balancing today's needs with tomorrow's obligations.

Transportation: Supports transportation improvements as part of smart growth that works for residents, balancing new development with infrastructure needs while improving quality of life and respecting existing neighborhoods.

Government accountability & ethics: Promotes transparent and responsive government: clear explanations of decisions, meaningful public participation, accountability, understandable communication, and welcoming different perspectives so residents feel informed and able to participate.

Housing: Fremont should use multiple levers for affordability: protect households now, increase housing availability, lower production costs, grow household capacity, and measure the affordability gap. Subsidy and deed-restricted housing help but structural affordability requires addressing the widening gap between market costs and purchasing power.

Transportation: Housing and mobility must be planned as one connected system. Practical alternatives must serve trips residents actually make, not merely assume a mode shift. Elected officials should establish outcomes, demand transparent cumulative analysis, and measure implementation rather than replacing professional engineering judgment.

campaign_platform_points: Housing: Build more affordable housing for working families, seniors, and people with disabilities, and expand transit-oriented development near BART and bus lines to reduce displacement and make housing more accessible.
Homelessness: Expand supportive housing and wraparound services to help unhoused individuals stay housed, building on Fremont's existing progress on homelessness.

Economy & cost of living: Ban private equity firms from purchasing residential property in Fremont to protect housing stock for individual families and first-time homebuyers rather than corporate investors.

Environment & climate: Oppose building AI data centers in Fremont, support solar canopies and panels on city property, require native species for all new city plantings, and develop community gardens on idle city land.
Immigration: Prohibit Fremont city staff and police from cooperating with or assisting ICE operations, consistent with California law, so all residents can interact with city government without fear.

Criminal justice & public safety: Ensure first responders have adequate training, equipment, mental health support, and community relationships, including investment in de-escalation training and mental health co-responder programs.

Transportation: Reduce traffic by partnering with navigation apps to steer cut-through traffic off neighborhood streets, improve signal timing, build roundabouts, create a pothole map with funded repair timeline, and add protected bike lanes.

Government accountability & ethics: Create a Section 115 Trust to set aside dedicated funds for pension obligations, conduct an independent cybersecurity audit and seismic risk assessment, and protect city investments from market volatility.

comments: Aziz as the Alameda Water District Chair has risen from serving the community and has the right experience to be a city council member

Other: Set strict goals for new development negotiations so incoming developers respect the town, with enforceable accountability metrics ensuring developers deliver on every promise, including funding parks and building community spaces that benefit residents directly.

Other: Deliver a new park to the Las Animas and Murray Avenue area to provide a vital shared community space bridging the new Ten South housing development and the neighborhood across Monterey Highway.

campaign_platform_points: Housing: Protect Measure D's 1.5% annual growth cap, establish a local-preference ordinance so affordable housing units go to Half Moon Bay residents first, create a live-work housing initiative for people who commute in, and encourage infill housing and ADUs.

Healthcare: Establish urgent care services on the Coastside, arguing the area currently lacks them and that road closures from earthquakes or wildfires could isolate residents for extended periods without nearby medical access.

Economy & cost of living: Improve downtown Main Street by adding gateway signage to direct visitors, improving parking, walkability, and cleanliness to support local businesses and keep the downtown area thriving.

Environment & climate: Address high wildfire risk by initiating a CDP process to thin brush in Frenchman's Creek, help neighborhoods plan for emergencies and evacuation, and replant medians along Highway 1.
Transportation: Complete the bike and pedestrian trail on the east side of Highway 1, extending it north to El Granada and south to Main Street, and make Highway 1 safer while keeping traffic moving.

Government accountability & ethics: Fight for public hearings on all major building projects in Half Moon Bay, oppose by-right and ministerial approval processes that bypass council and planning commission input, and be more cost-conscious about City Attorney time at meetings.

Other: Push to complete a public swimming pool on the Coastside, noting the school district has already approved it and the community has discussed it for decades, framing it as a long-overdue public amenity.

Housing: Resist state pressure to approve large housing projects without local input, criticizing the Density Bonus Law and by-right process as allowing developers to bypass public hearings and community compromise on height, parking, and safety.

campaign_platform_points: Criminal justice & public safety: Dion Bailey commits to continuing to prioritize public safety investments in Hercules so the city remains a safe place for families to live.

Other: Bailey pledges to build on recent upgrades to the gym and swim center, Refugio Valley Park's picnic areas, and Foxboro Park's courts and playground, continuing investment in parks and recreation facilities.

Economy & cost of living: Bailey supports small businesses through programs like the Shop Local Gift Card Program while keeping Hercules on solid financial footing, combining local economic support with fiscal responsibility.

Transportation: Bailey advocates advancing traffic calming on Village Parkway and John Muir Parkway, pavement rehabilitation on Sycamore Avenue and Falcon Way, and reliable, accessible transit through his role on the WestCAT Board.

Protect existing affordable and naturally affordable housing and enforce tenant-protection laws.

Education: Deepen the city's partnership with Belle Haven Elementary and Ravenswood district, expand after-school and summer programs at the Belle Haven Community Center, formalize a written joint-use agreement for shared facilities, add a college-and-career advising corner at the Belle Haven Library, and press for a public plan for the empty TIDE Academy campus.

Economy & cost of living: Recruit locally-serving commercial development (grocery, pharmacy, bank, clinic) to District 1, carry forward the Willow Village vision or a similar plan, reinvest new sales-tax revenue into city services, and study repurposing Bohannon Office Park as a mixed-use destination with housing, retail, and jobs.

Transportation: Push to build the Dumbarton corridor busway and protected bike path to Caltrain sooner, address cut-through traffic on Hamilton, Newbridge, and Chilco streets with calming and enforcement, and move street sweeping to overnight hours so debris no longer clogs storm drains.

Systematically sunset obsolete or unenforced ordinances. Use AI to reduce manual busywork in city operations. Build a single consolidated app for all city services.

Environment & climate: Close the tree-canopy gap north of Highway 101 with planting and maintenance to cool streets, improve air quality, and manage stormwater. Prepare for El Niño flooding. Criminal justice & public safety: Implement proactive code enforcement against illegal dumping, derelict lots, broken-down vehicles, and long-neglected properties in District 1, rather than relying solely on complaint-driven cleanup, to keep the neighborhood looking cared for and deter blight.

Economy & cost of living: Revitalize Downtown Menlo Park by fixing crumbling sidewalks and neglected streetscape, modernizing allowed business types on Santa Cruz Avenue to include community-serving and small-scale commercial recreation, launching Fourth Fridays live music events, and investing in infrastructure to keep the commercial core vibrant.

Government accountability & ethics: Address Menlo Park's structural budget deficit through fiscal responsibility, logical decision-making, accurate data, and effective execution. As Finance and Audit Commission Chair, she emphasizes analytical rigor and management metrics for creating government efficiencies.

Transportation: Expand traffic safety tools for neighborhoods and schools, including implementing speed limit reductions under AB 43. Restart and expand the Slow Streets Program using faster, less expensive pilots validated by other municipalities to make streets safer for kids, walkers, and bikers.

Environment & climate: Protect Menlo Park's parks, heritage trees, open spaces, and neighborhoods through active stewardship. She previously organized neighbors to save a 90-year-old heritage tree from developer destruction and advocates for preserving the physical character of the city.

Government accountability & ethics: Commit to listening to residents and valuing their quality of life, contrasting with her view that the current City Council dismisses neighborhood concerns. She wants decisions that make sense to the people who have to live with them.

Housing: Menlo Park's most critical housing shortfall is in very-low-income units (at or below 50% of area median income), with 603 more permits needed by 2031. The campaign's central priority is closing that specific gap rather than treating all affordable housing categories as equivalent.

Housing: The city should use its leverage during project review to deepen income restrictions in already-approved developments (e.g., Parkline's 154 units at 60% AMI) to very-low-income levels, costing roughly $90,000 per unit, rather than relying solely on new construction from scratch.

campaign_platform_points: Economy & cost of living: Hold non-tax-paying regional agencies (SFO, SFPUC, BART, Caltrain) accountable for the heavy financial and environmental strains they place on Millbrae, which has borne regional burdens for over 100 years.

Economy & cost of living: Oppose SFPUC converting the Outdoor Supply Hardware site on El Camino Real into a heavy-vehicle corporate yard; preserve the land for commercial use to balance Millbrae's tax base.

Economy & cost of living: Actively push back on costly SFPUC projects that have driven Millbrae's retail water rates to the second highest in San Mateo County, and resist subsidizing other Hetch Hetchy customers.

Environment & climate: Create a Habitat Conservation Protection Area so Millbrae can receive regional mitigation funding from businesses and agencies to reduce flooding and sea-level-rise risks while providing public access to nature.

Government accountability & ethics: Restore the annual transparent public council goal-setting process that has been absent since 2023, covering public safety, climate, and care for vulnerable residents, as a critical step in open governance.

Economy & cost of living: Maximize tax revenue from remaining commercial zones, including ensuring a new hotel is built on the old El Rancho site, to compensate for the massive amounts of tax-exempt land owned by regional agencies.

Transportation: Implement rapid-response traffic calming measures to protect residential streets from regional cut-through traffic, and advocate for one-way conversions on narrow residential roads to eliminate dangerous 3-point turns.
Environment & climate: Enforce strict environmental mitigation within the Eastside Specific Plan to curb flooding, heat waves, SFO noise, and air pollution affecting Millbrae residents.

campaign_platform_points: Economy & cost of living: Opposes any new or future tax increases, citing Milpitas already having one of the highest sales tax rates in the county. Commits to finding new revenue opportunities and cutting wasteful spending using business experience.

Transportation: Will modernize traffic-signal timings, reduce regional cut-through traffic through neighborhoods, and request an updated safety study to identify optimal locations for stop signs, traffic signals, and speed bumps to maximize flow and protect residents.

Housing: Will reassess future housing, retail, and business needs while measuring traffic impact and preserving hillsides. Will work with legislators to draft legislation helping small cities preserve retail and business spaces while providing responsible affordable housing without converting business zones to housing-only.

Criminal justice & public safety: Supports strong law enforcement and firm consequences for car theft, drug dealing, break-ins, and violent crime, while expanding rehabilitation for nonviolent first-time offenders. Will fight for neighborhood security cameras, improved street lighting in hotspots, and increased police patrols.
Other: Will prioritize investment in roads, utilities, public facilities, parks, and playgrounds to create a better Milpitas for children, seniors, and families.

Jobs & labor: Economic focus on attracting and approving premier businesses that offer high-paying jobs to raise quality of life without adding burden to residents. Cites support for Amazon fulfillment center, light industrial center, and Sierra Way food park as examples.

Government accountability & ethics: Formally pledges non-partisan governance, refusing any political party endorsement. Campaign rejects corporate PAC money, political nonprofits, social-welfare groups, labor unions, and trade or business association contributions, committing to accountability to residents only.

Healthcare: Turner launched the Healthy Morgan Hill initiative built on four pillars—natural movement, nutrition, social connections, and self-care—integrating wellness into city policy and infrastructure planning.

An early advocate for calling for a ceasefire in Gaza.  Or we know they are part of the Muslim community, or has personally been a strong champion for our cause such as leading / introducing a ceasefire resolution. criteria.F: Shields Israel and a strong defender of Israel or has endorsements from Hindutva or Zionist organizations (other than JStreetPAC)
